timeline.label: Big Bethel congregation organized, the oldest African American congregation in Atlanta
Wheat Street Baptist Church founded
Ebenezer Baptist Church founded
Wheat Street renamed Auburn Avenue
Henry A. Rucker builds the Rucker Building, Atlanta's first Black-owned office building
Alonzo Herndon founds the insurance company that became Atlanta Life
The Atlanta Race Riot erupts in September; Black businesses relocate to Auburn Avenue for safety
Heman E. Perry founds Standard Life Insurance
Citizens Trust Bank opens on Auburn Avenue (August 16)
W. A. Scott II founds the Atlanta World (August 5); it becomes the Atlanta Daily World, the first successful Black daily, by 1932
Martin Luther King, Jr. is born at 501 Auburn Avenue (January 15)
Fortune magazine calls Auburn Avenue "the richest Negro street in the world"
Sweet Auburn Historic District designated a National Historic Landmark
The King National Historic Site is established and HDDC is founded
An NPS assessment finds 47 percent of the district's historic buildings lost since 1976

questions.q: Which statement about Sweet Auburn is accurate?
options: It was an incorporated Black town with its own mayor and council
It is a historic district and neighborhood within Atlanta that was never an incorporated town
It was founded by John Wesley Dobbs in 1893
It became a National Historic Landmark in 1956
questions.explain: The dossier answers the town fields honestly for a district: Sweet Auburn was never incorporated and sits inside Atlanta's Old Fourth Ward.

questions.q: Why did Auburn Avenue become the anchor of Black business in Atlanta?
options: The city government designated it a Black business zone
As Jim Crow law hardened, Atlanta's Black population and businesses were pushed into the corridor east of downtown
John Wesley Dobbs bought most of the street's property
A fire destroyed every other Black business district in the city
questions.explain: The chapter says that as Jim Crow hardened in the 1890s and 1900s, Black residents and businesses were pushed into the corridor east of downtown, and Auburn Avenue became its east-side anchor.

questions.q: Who coined the name "Sweet Auburn"?
options: Alonzo Herndon
John Wesley Dobbs
Henry A. Rucker
Adam Daniel Williams
questions.explain: Civic leader John Wesley Dobbs coined "Sweet Auburn," in reference to the prosperity and opportunity the neighborhood afforded, and served as the avenue's unofficial mayor.

questions.q: According to the chapter's dated spine, what set off the September 1906 Atlanta Race Riot?
options: A dispute over the renaming of Wheat Street
Newspaper reports that inflamed white mobs
The opening of a competing bank on the avenue
The Great Atlanta Fire of 1917
questions.explain: The spine records that the riot erupted after newspaper reports inflamed white mobs; at least 25 Black Atlantans were killed and more than 70 people injured.

questions.q: What did Alonzo Herndon found in 1905?
options: Citizens Trust Bank
Standard Life Insurance
The insurance company that became Atlanta Life
The Atlanta Daily World
questions.explain: Herndon, born enslaved and by then a successful barbershop owner, founded his insurance company in 1905, the seed of Atlanta Life Insurance Company.

questions.q: Historian Gary Pomerantz gave the avenue's financial core a name. What did he call Atlanta Life Insurance, Standard Life Insurance, and Citizens Trust Bank together?
options: The Fervent Five
The three-legged stool of Black finance
The richest street in the world
The civic capital of Atlanta
questions.explain: Pomerantz's phrase for the avenue's financial core is the "three-legged stool of Black finance," naming the two insurance companies and the bank.

questions.q: In 1956, Fortune magazine described Auburn Avenue as what?
options: "the richest Negro street in the world"
"the capital of Black America"
"the loveliest village of the plain"
"the most interesting Negro town in the United States"
questions.explain: Fortune's 1956 description, the capstone of the peak years, called Auburn Avenue "the richest Negro street in the world."

questions.q: Why was the 1906 massacre important in causing Auburn Avenue's rise as a Black business district?
options: It destroyed the avenue itself, which was then rebuilt with federal landmark money

Before 1906, Black businesses operated in a substantially integrated downtown; after the massacre they relocated to Auburn Avenue for safety, and segregation concentrated Black spending there for half a century
It led directly to the founding of Citizens Trust Bank that same year
It persuaded Fortune magazine to praise the street
questions.explain: The chapter keeps the paradox plain: the violence pushed Black businesses out of the integrated downtown, and segregation then held a captive market's spending on the avenue.

questions.q: What structural change from the mid-1960s drained the avenue?
options: The Great Atlanta Fire of 1917
As legal barriers fell, shopkeepers and residents moved to other parts of the city, while construction of the Downtown Connector divided the district
The Atlanta Daily World closed its offices
The Sweet Auburn Festival was cancelled
questions.explain: Desegregation let businesses and residents disperse across the city, the Downtown Connector (Interstates 75/85) took the district's western blocks, and disinvestment followed.

questions.q: What did the 2021 National Park Service assessment find about the district's historic buildings?
options: Nearly all of them survived intact
Sweet Auburn had lost 47 percent of its historic buildings since the 1976 landmark designation
The district had doubled its historic building stock
Every landmark building was occupied and in use
questions.explain: The 2021 assessment found 47 percent of historic buildings lost since 1976, with the Atlanta Life building, the Butler Street YMCA, and the Walden Building vacant and at risk.

questions.q: Which pair of events does the chapter date to 1980?
options: The first Sweet Auburn Festival and the founding of the APEX Museum
The Martin Luther King, Jr. National Historic Site was established, and HDDC was founded by Coretta Scott King and Christine King Farris
The Atlanta Streetcar was completed and the research library opened
The landmark designation and the founding of Sweet Auburn Works
questions.explain: In 1980 the King historic site was established on October 10, and the Historic District Development Corporation was founded the same year to revitalize the residential area.

questions.q: At what address stands the Birth Home of Martin Luther King, Jr.?
options: 145 Auburn Avenue
501 Auburn Avenue
220 Auburn Avenue
101 Auburn Avenue
questions.explain: The Birth Home at 501 Auburn Avenue was built in 1895 and purchased by the Reverend A. D. Williams in 1909.

questions.q: What is the chapter's honest summary of the district today?
options: A fully restored reconstruction of the peak years
The landmarks are real and visitable and the churches still worship, but the commercial street between the landmarks remains thinner than its history deserves
The district is closed to visitors pending restoration
The Curb Market no longer trades
questions.explain: The chapter closes on that balance: working landmarks and living churches, with landmark buildings vacant and nearly half the historic fabric gone since 1976.

questions.q: The song's intro credits Dobbs with the street being the "richest." What does the annotation say is the accurate record?
options: Dobbs coined both the name "Sweet Auburn" and the "richest" line
Dobbs coined the name "Sweet Auburn"; the "richest" wording is Fortune magazine's, from 1956
Fortune coined the name and Dobbs wrote the "richest" line
Neither attribution can be checked against any source
questions.explain: The annotation calls the intro line a merge of two attributions: Dobbs coined "Sweet Auburn," Fortune printed the "richest" wording in 1956, and verse 2 assigns each correctly.

questions.q: The lyric runs "1906 riots scatter seeds" together with "Wheat Street flip to Auburn." What does the annotation say about that sequence?
options: Both events happened in 1906, so the line is exact
The renaming dates to 1893 and Black businesses stood on the street by 1900, so the song compresses the sequence rather than stating the chronology
The renaming never actually happened
The riot happened in 1893, the year of the renaming
questions.explain: The massacre did concentrate Black business on the avenue, but the renaming was 1893 and businesses were present by 1900; the annotation names the line a compression, not the chronology.

questions.q: Which source in this chapter is a federal document in the public domain?
options: The Atlanta Daily World run in the ProQuest database
The National Register of Historic Places nomination form for the Sweet Auburn Historic District (1976)
The circa 1945 photograph held by the Atlanta History Center
The Samuel W. Williams Collection at the research library
questions.explain: The chapter lists the 1976 National Register nomination form as a federal document in the public domain; the photograph is copyrighted and linked only.

questions.q: Why does this dossier end with a section headed "Conflicts between sources, recorded not smoothed"?
options: To make the dossier longer for the curriculum
Because where sources disagree, the dossier carries both versions and flags the variance instead of quietly picking one
Because no two sources agree on anything in the district's history
Because the bibliography was left unfinished
questions.explain: From the landmark year to the casualty counts, the dossier records disagreements openly, with the sources named, rather than smoothing them into a single claim.

timeline.label: Townsite established in August; opened for settlement September 26
Formal opening of the townsite (September 22)
Boley incorporated (May 11); the Boley Progress newspaper begins publication
Farmers and Merchants Bank organized
Oklahoma statehood; Boley counts 824 residents
Booker T. Washington publishes his account of Boley in The Outlook (January 4)
A booster pamphlet advertises the town; its 4,000 figure counts the surrounding farm trade territory
The three-story Masonic Temple is completed by about this year
First National Bank of Boley opens, the first Black-owned bank to hold a national charter
Bill Pickett, the famous Black cowboy, films at Boley
The Pretty Boy Floyd gang's robbery of the Farmers and Merchants Bank fails (November 23); D. J. Turner is killed
The railroad through Boley is dissolved and the line dismantled (1939 to 1940)
Boley Historic District added to the National Register and designated a National Historic Landmark (May 15)
The John H. Lilley Correctional Center opens

questions.q: Which statement about Boley today is accurate?
options: It was never incorporated and no longer exists
It is still an incorporated town, one of thirteen surviving Oklahoma Black towns out of more than fifty founded; its historic district is a National Historic Landmark
It is now a neighborhood inside Oklahoma City
It was destroyed and never rebuilt
questions.explain: The header records Boley as a still-incorporated town, one of thirteen survivors of Oklahoma's more than fifty Black towns, with its district a National Historic Landmark since 1975.

questions.q: On whose land did Boley's townsite stand?
options: Land leased from the Choctaw Nation
The Creek freedwoman allotment of Abigail Barnett
A railroad land grant sold to the founders
Homestead claims filed by the town company
questions.explain: The townsite stood on the Creek freedwoman allotment of Abigail Barnett, daughter of James Barnett, in what was then Indian Territory.

questions.q: What was J. B. Boley's founding argument for the town?
options: That Oklahoma's oil would make Black settlers rich
That Black people were generally convinced they were incapable of self-government but had never had a fair chance to prove themselves
That the town should copy Tulsa's Greenwood district
That farming should be replaced by industry
questions.explain: Washington preserved the argument: Boley and his backers founded the town to demonstrate Black self-government, on land allotted to Creek freedmen.

questions.q: What distinguished the First National Bank of Boley, organized in 1921?
options: It was the largest bank in Oklahoma
It was the first Black-owned bank in the United States to hold a national charter
It was the only bank Booker T. Washington ever visited
It survived the 1932 robbery without any loss
questions.explain: The chapter records the First National Bank of Boley as the first Black-owned bank in the country carrying a national charter.

questions.q: The chapter calls the Boley Progress (1905 to 1916) more than a newspaper. What was its second role?
options: It was the town's official census record
It was the recruiting engine whose reports and photographs of Black prosperity drew settlers from across the South
It printed the town's bank notes
It served as the railroad's advertising sheet
questions.explain: The Progress was both chronicle and recruiter: its issues carried the town's story and images of Black prosperity to prospective settlers in the South.

questions.q: How did Booker T. Washington describe Boley in The Outlook in 1908?
options: "the richest Negro street in the world"
"the loveliest village of the plain"
"the most enterprising, and in many ways the most interesting, of the Negro towns in the United States"
"the first Black-incorporated town in America"
questions.explain: Washington's January 4, 1908 account called Boley "the most enterprising, and in many ways the most interesting, of the Negro towns in the United States."

questions.q: The booster figure of about 4,000 people by 1911 is often quoted as Boley's peak population. What does the chapter say it actually counted?
options: The town's official census count
The town plus its surrounding farm trade territory; the highest census count inside the town itself was 1,334 in 1910
Visitors at the annual reunion
Residents of all thirteen Oklahoma Black towns combined
questions.explain: The 4,000 figure belongs to the town with its trade territory; counted on their own terms, federal censuses give 824 in 1907 and a high of 1,334 in 1910.

questions.q: Boley's economy rested on a single architecture. What was it, and how did it fail?
options: Oil and tourism; the wells ran dry in the 1920s
Cotton farming served by one railroad; farm prices fell through the 1920s, the Depression finished the banks, and the railroad was dissolved in 1939
Banking and insurance; federal regulation closed the banks
Ranching and rodeos; the rodeo was banned in 1930
questions.explain: The chapter says cotton prices, the Depression, and the 1939 loss of the railroad formed one squeeze on a farm-and-rail town, and Boley shrank with the countryside around it.

questions.q: Why did the November 23, 1932 robbery of the Farmers and Merchants Bank fail completely?
options: The vault was empty that day

Cashier D. J. Turner sounded the alarm as he was killed, H. C. McCormick shot George Birdwell dead from inside the vault, and armed townspeople stopped the rest; Charles "Pretty Boy" Floyd had warned his men to stay away from Boley
Federal agents happened to be in town
The gang surrendered when the bank president negotiated with them
questions.explain: The chapter records that the robbery failed completely: Turner died raising the alarm, McCormick fired from the vault, and the town's armed response did the rest.

questions.q: By what hard measures does the chapter say Boley survived?
options: It kept a railroad station and a daily newspaper
It stayed incorporated and self-governing, kept electing its own town government, and is one of only thirteen Oklahoma all-Black towns still existing
Its population returned to the 1910 peak
It annexed neighboring towns to stay viable
questions.explain: Survival here is institutional: same town, same charter, same self-government, one of thirteen survivors of the more than fifty that were founded.

questions.q: How does the dossier say Boley's post-1980 census rebounds must be read?
options: As families returning to farm
As an artifact: the roughly 800 inmates of the John H. Lilley Correctional Center, opened in 1983, are counted as Boley residents
As growth from the rodeo's popularity
As a counting error in the 1990 census only
questions.explain: The chapter warns that the rebound is the prison population inside the town limits, not civilians moving back; the honest civilian figure stays small.

questions.q: What is Boley's signature gathering?
options: The Boley Rodeo and Bar-B-Que Festival, held each Memorial Day weekend and billed as the nation's oldest African American community-based rodeo
An annual reenactment of the 1932 bank robbery
The Oklahoma Black Towns reunion in Oklahoma City
A Booker T. Washington birthday pageant each January
questions.explain: The rodeo, run since 1961 by the Boley Chamber of Commerce, is the town's signature gathering and its most legible claim on the present tense.

questions.q: The lyric names a "Farmers and Teachers State Bank." What does the annotation say?
options: The name is accurate and appears in the bank's charter
No such institution appears in any source; the documented name is the Farmers and Merchants Bank, and the lyric line is flagged as an uncorrected error left in the shipped record
The name was the bank's name after 1932
The bank was renamed by the town council in 1921
questions.explain: Section 2 documents the Farmers and Merchants Bank; the annotation marks the lyric's bank name as an error and carries the correction rather than silently rewriting the record.

questions.q: Which decline cause in the song is NOT supported by the dossier's record?
options: Collapsed farm prices
Dried-up oil
The railroad's abandonment in 1939
The Great Depression
questions.explain: The annotation marks "dried-up oil" poetic but not documented; Sections 4 and 5 record the farm economy's collapse, the Depression, and the 1939 rail abandonment.

questions.q: Which source does the chapter call "the single most important contemporary account" of Boley?
options: Booker T. Washington, "Boley, a Negro Town in the West," The Outlook, January 4, 1908
The 1911 booster pamphlet, "Boley, Indian Territory Oklahoma"
The Oklahoma Historical Society encyclopedia entry
Norman L. Crockett's 1979 scholarly history
questions.explain: Washington's Outlook article, reporting his 1905 visit, is the chapter's first-listed primary source: the founding argument, the population figures, and the cotton-gin description all come from it.

questions.q: What did the Perplexity library search establish about Boley?
options: It produced Boley-specific facts not found anywhere else
Boley appears only as list mentions inside two broader town threads; the library added no Boley-specific dated facts, and the audit caught one misfiling under Boley's name
It contradicted the town's founding date
It held the only copy of the Boley Progress
questions.explain: The dossier states the gap plainly: Boley's dated facts come from Washington, the Oklahoma Historical Society, and NPS records, not from the Perplexity library.

timeline.label: The Nicodemus Town Company is organized in April; settlers arrive from June, the main Kentucky party in September
First Emancipation Day celebration on August 1; the post office opens with Z. T. Fletcher as first postmaster
The Town Company is abolished in April; the Exoduster migration follows
Graham County is organized (April 1) with John DePrad as county clerk
Edward P. McCabe is elected Kansas state auditor
The Western Cyclone publishes its first issue (May 13); the town receives title to its site (June 6); an Emancipation crowd of 4,000 to 5,000 is reported
The Bank of Nicodemus is established and the stone schoolhouse (District No. 1) is built
The Union Pacific builds through Bogue, miles south, and the railroad bypass becomes final
The Dust Bowl reaches the plains settlements
The Nicodemus post office is discontinued
The Nicodemus Historic District is designated a National Historic Landmark
Angela Bates founds the Nicodemus Historical Society
Congress establishes Nicodemus National Historic Site (November), preserving the five structures

questions.q: How is Nicodemus governed today?
options: By a mayor and town council, like Eatonville
It was never incorporated; it is an unincorporated community governed through Nicodemus Township in Graham County, and the townsite is a National Historic Site
Directly by the National Park Service
It is not governed; the site is abandoned
questions.explain: The header carries the never-incorporated fact plainly: township government, a resident community, and a National Historic Site established in November 1996.

questions.q: Why was the Nicodemus Town Company organized in April 1877?
options: To build a railroad station for the Kansas Pacific
So Black settlers, mostly from Kentucky, could own land, vote, and govern themselves at the moment Reconstruction was collapsing
To recruit labor for Graham County wheat farms
To found a college on the plains
questions.explain: The chapter ties the founding to the end of Reconstruction: the company, led by the Reverend W. H. Smith and Benjamin Carr, offered land ownership and self-government in Kansas.

questions.q: What did the main Kentucky party find when it arrived in September 1877?
options: A built town with a hotel and stores
A paper plat and open prairie: no houses, no trees; families wintered in dugouts, and about sixty of some three hundred settlers returned to Kentucky at once
A railroad depot and a stocked warehouse
A fortified settlement of sod houses
questions.explain: The chapter records the gap between promotion and fact: a surveyed townsite on treeless prairie, a winter of dugouts, and roughly a fifth of the party turning back.

questions.q: What did Edward P. McCabe's 1882 election say about Nicodemus at its strongest?
options: He became the town's first mayor
He was elected Kansas state auditor, the highest elective office then held by a Black man in any state outside the South
He was appointed postmaster by the governor
He won a seat in the U.S. Congress
questions.explain: The political spine runs from John Niles in 1877 to McCabe's 1882 state auditor win, alongside the township offices and DePrad's county clerkship.

questions.q: Why does August 1, 1878 matter in Nicodemus?
options: The town company was abolished that day
The first Emancipation Day celebration was held then, an observance the community has carried every year since (today's Homecoming)
The railroad arrived that day
Graham County was organized that day
questions.explain: Emancipation Day began August 1, 1878, the same summer the post office opened; the chapter calls it the community institution rather than a town business.

questions.q: Why does the dossier refuse to print a single peak population for Nicodemus?
options: No census was ever taken in Kansas

The surviving counts measure different things (townsite, township, and county) and still conflict, 700 reported for 1880 against a census reading of 484 in the county and 260 in the township, so the peak population is carried as NOT ESTABLISHED
The records were destroyed in the Dust Bowl
The town company hid the figures from recruiters
questions.explain: Conflict 1 in Section 9 is the stated reason: the numbers rest on different units and different political incentives, so the dossier carries no single peak figure.

questions.q: When does the chapter place Nicodemus's peak era?
options: 1877 to 1879, the founding winters
Roughly 1886 through the first decade of the 1900s
The Dust Bowl years
After the 1996 historic site designation
questions.explain: The chapter dates the fullest documented life, two newspapers, the bank, the stone schoolhouse, to the mid-1880s through the 1900s, before the bypass drained the trade.

questions.q: Why was the railroad bypass of 1888 important in causing Nicodemus's decline?
options: The town refused a depot on principle and trade simply followed the refusal

Plains prosperity ran on rail access: the town voted $16,000 in bonds and courted three companies, but the Union Pacific built through Bogue instead, and businesses and the county's trade drained to the rail towns
The bypass happened after the town had already emptied
The railroad arrived but refused to stop for freight
questions.explain: The chapter is explicit that the failure was not effort: bonds were voted and companies courted, and when the line ran through Bogue in 1888 the commercial future moved with it.

questions.q: What earlier blow had already thinned the settler base before the bypass?
options: The post office closure
The winter blizzard of 1885 destroyed about 40 percent of the wheat crop and started an exodus by settlers who had arrived expecting more
The abolition of the Town Company
A tornado destroyed the schoolhouse
questions.explain: The chapter pairs the two blows: the 1885 blizzard began the defections, and the 1888 bypass made the decline permanent.

questions.q: What did Angela Bates's six years of work produce in November 1996?
options: A rebuilt railroad spur to Bogue
Congress established Nicodemus National Historic Site, protecting the townsite and its five structures as a unit of the National Park System
Reincorporation of the town
A state park at the townsite
questions.explain: The chapter dates the designation campaign from Bates's 1988 Historical Society to the November 1996 act of Congress, the institutional form survival takes for an unincorporated town.

questions.q: When and why did the Nicodemus post office close?
options: It closed in 1888 when the railroad bypassed the town
It was discontinued in 1953, an economic decision from Washington that the chapter treats as a later chapter of the same decline
It never closed; it still operates daily
It closed when the Bank of Nicodemus failed
questions.explain: The post office that opened in 1878 was discontinued in 1953; the chapter names the closure a bookend of decline, not a founding-era event.

questions.q: The Park Service pairs each of the five preserved buildings with a theme. Which pairing is correct?
options: First Baptist Church = government
School District No. 1 = education
The St. Francis Hotel = religion
Township Hall = commerce
questions.explain: The pairings run: AME Church, religion; St. Francis Hotel, commerce; Township Hall, community; First Baptist Church, family; School District No. 1, education.

questions.q: The annotation flags the lyric "Prayin' with the Osage." Why?
options: The Osage are documented as the town's founders
No source in the dossier mentions the Osage in connection with Nicodemus; the documented help was Kansas Pacific relief supplies shipped free in 1878 to 1879, so the line is carried as unverified
The line misdates the first winter
The Osage objected to the song in writing
questions.explain: Under the dossier's rule that religious and descriptive color cannot be presented as history without a source, the Osage line is flagged rather than repeated as fact.

questions.q: The song says "we flipped Graham County." What does the annotation say actually happened?
options: Black voters held every county office by 1882

Specific offices were won inside a majority-white county (convention delegate, county clerk, justices of the peace, state auditor), and the 1880 county-seat vote was lost to Millbrook, so the phrase overstates a real record
The county was never contested at any level
The phrase refers to a land purchase, not politics
questions.explain: The annotation keeps the achievements and corrects the scale: real offices won, a real county-seat loss, inside a county whose population was majority white.

questions.q: Which account does the chapter treat as the standard first-person record of the settlers' arrival?
options: The Nicodemus Western Cyclone's first issue
Mrs. Williana Hickman's 1878 account, "That is Nicodemus," preserved in The Black West (1971)
W. R. Hill's 1877 promotional circular
The 1890 Kansas state census
questions.explain: Hickman's testimony of the September 1877 arrival was first printed for a general reader in William Loren Katz's The Black West in 1971 and is the standard arrival account.

questions.q: Why does Section 9 flag the description "Exoduster farm colony" for the 1877 founding?
options: The Exodusters settled in Oklahoma, not Kansas
The 1877 founding predates the 1879 Exoduster wave by two years; the Exodusters are part of the town's growth story, not its origin event
No Nicodemus settler ever farmed
The term Exoduster was invented by the Park Service
questions.explain: Conflict 7 states the standing rule: two years is two years, and the label moves the founding into a migration it preceded.

timeline.label: Joseph C. Clarke persuades Josiah Eaton to sell 22 acres; the land is cut into 48 lots offered only to Black buyers, and St. Lawrence AME is founded
The settlement is renamed Eatonville
Eatonville incorporates on August 15; 27 registered Black electors vote it in and elect an all-Black slate, Joseph E. Boger as first mayor
The post office opens; the Eatonville Speaker advertises "a Negro City Governed by Negroes"
The Hurston family arrives; Zora Neale Hurston is three years old
John Hurston is called as pastor of Macedonia Missionary Baptist Church
Hurston publishes Mules and Men, her folklore collection rooted in the town
Their Eyes Were Watching God is published
The county takes control of the Hungerford campus (1950 to 1951) under an education deed restriction
The Association to Preserve the Eatonville Community (P.E.C.) is organized against the Kennedy Boulevard widening
The first ZORA! Festival is held and the Zora Neale Hurston National Museum of Fine Arts opens
The Eatonville Historic District is listed on the National Register (February 3)
Hungerford Preparatory closes; the school buildings are later demolished
The National Trust names Eatonville one of America's 11 Most Endangered Historic Places (May 1)
The Orange County School Board votes to sell the Hungerford land to Dr. Phillips Charities (January 13)

questions.q: Which statement describes Eatonville as the dossier carries it?
options: An unincorporated neighborhood of Orlando
A still-incorporated town with a mayor-council government, whose motto is "The Town That Freedom Built"
A town destroyed in the 1920s and later rebuilt as a museum
A district administered by Orange County since 1951
questions.explain: The header records continuous incorporation: mayor-council government today, building permits and its own police department, under the motto "The Town That Freedom Built."

questions.q: Why did Eatonville's land become available to Black buyers in 1881?
options: A federal land grant reserved it for freedmen

At Orlando realtor Joseph C. Clarke's urging, Union veteran Josiah Eaton sold 22 acres that were surveyed into 48 lots offered only to Black buyers, at a moment when prejudice was blocking Clarke's other sales
The town won the land in a court settlement
Zora Neale Hurston's father purchased the tract
questions.explain: The chapter is plain that the founding was a real-estate transaction across the color line: Eaton sold, Clarke subdivided, and the lots were offered only to Black buyers under a temperance covenant.

questions.q: What happened on August 15, 1887?
options: The Hungerford school opened its doors
The town's 27 registered Black electors voted to incorporate and elected an all-Black slate of officers, Joseph E. Boger as first mayor
The post office opened under an Eatonville name
The first ZORA! Festival was held
questions.explain: Peacemaking judge E. K. Foster supervised the vote and swore the officers in; the chapter notes the incorporation certified Black men voting and governing under Florida law in 1887.

questions.q: What kind of institution was the Hungerford school?
options: A one-room county elementary school
A private boarding school modeled on Tuskegee, which by 1927 housed more than 100 boarding students alongside day and night students
A seminary for training ministers only
A Rosenwald elementary school for the town's children
questions.explain: Russell C. Calhoun and his wife Mary, Tuskegee graduates, ran Hungerford on the Tuskegee model: academic and industrial courses, a working campus, and service to a region, not just a town.

questions.q: How did the Eatonville Speaker advertise the town in 1889?
options: "The Town That Freedom Built"
"a Negro City Governed by Negroes"
"the richest Negro street in the world"
"the most enterprising Negro town in the United States"
questions.explain: The 1889 advertisement in the town's own newspaper is quoted in the chapter as the founders writing their own description of what they had made.

questions.q: Which statement about Zora Neale Hurston and Eatonville is accurate?
options: She was born in Eatonville in 1891

She was born in Notasulga, Alabama, on January 7, 1891, and arrived in Eatonville in 1894 at age three; the town became the raw material for Mules and Men (1935) and Their Eyes Were Watching God (1937)
She moved to Eatonville as an adult to research folklore
She served as the town's mayor in the 1930s
questions.explain: The chapter corrects the compressed version: Alabama-born, Eatonville-raised from age three, and the town's talk, church, and school became the substance of her major work.

questions.q: What was Eatonville's demographic peak, and when?
options: 824 residents at statehood in 1907
2,432 residents in the 2000 census, the highest modern count before two decades of drift downward
About 4,000 in the 1911 booster years
The town has never been counted by the census
questions.explain: The decennial series in Section 9 peaks at 2,432 in 2000; later counts settle near 2,300, which the chapter frames as community stability rather than growth.

questions.q: Why was the fight over widening Kennedy Boulevard important in causing the ZORA! Festival?
options: The festival was the county's apology for the widening

Residents organized P.E.C. in 1987 against a five-lane widening meant to erase the historic corridor; the widening was cancelled, and the festival was launched in 1990 as the winning side's awareness campaign
The widening was completed and the festival marks its route
Alice Walker proposed the festival at a town council meeting in 1980
questions.explain: The chapter calls the festival a defensive weapon that outlived the fight: organized against the road in 1987, cancelled road, first festival in 1990, Hurston reframed from local memory to the town's public argument.

questions.q: What is the Hungerford land's history in one line?
options: It was sold to developers in 1887 and built over

The county took the campus in 1950 to 1951 for about $16,000 under a deed restriction for education; the school closed in 2009, the buildings were demolished, and about 100 acres of restricted land remain
It is still operated by Tuskegee graduates
It became the site of the Zora Neale Hurston museum
questions.explain: The chapter traces the tract from private Black boarding school to county hands under trust terms, to a closed school and a vacant, deed-restricted parcel at the town's edge.

questions.q: What did the Eatonville Town Council do on February 7, 2023?
options: It approved the developer's rezoning of the Hungerford land
It rejected the developer's requested plan amendments and zoning changes for the Hungerford land, a decision P.E.C. later cited when it sued the School Board
It voted to sell the land to Dr. Phillips Charities
It dissolved the town government
questions.explain: The chapter records the 2023 rejection as the town keeping its side of the argument, even as the School Board, which owns the land, moved toward its own disposition.

questions.q: What did the Orange County School Board vote on January 13, 2026?
options: To rebuild Hungerford Preparatory on the site
To sell about 117 acres to Dr. Phillips Charities for $14 million, with up to $13 million forgiven against community milestones; the chapter notes the closing itself is not verified in its sources
To return the land to the town without conditions
To list the land on the National Register
questions.explain: The vote is recorded with its terms and its caveat: a purchase-and-sale agreement approved, a closing not verified, and the land's future still argued from several sides.

questions.q: What does the chapter say about the Hurston museum and the Moseley House?
options: Both closed when Hungerford shut in 2009

The Zora Neale Hurston National Museum of Fine Arts opened in 1990 on Kennedy Boulevard, and the Moseley House (1888) is the town's second-oldest structure, home of Hurston's best friend Matilda Moseley
The museum is located in Orlando, not Eatonville
The Moseley House was demolished for the road widening
questions.explain: The chapter places the museum on East Kennedy Boulevard in the historic district and the Moseley House on Calhoun Avenue, both visitable anchors of the town Hurston described.

questions.q: The lyric calls Eatonville "the first Black-incorporated town." What does the annotation say?
options: The claim is exact; no earlier example exists

It is an overclaim: Brooklyn, Illinois (1873) and Princeville, North Carolina (1885) predate it; the supported claim is among the first self-governing all-Black municipalities in the United States, continuously incorporated since 1887
The claim fails because Eatonville never incorporated
The annotation removes the line from the song
questions.explain: The annotation adjudicates the superlative with the counterexamples and keeps the narrower, documented claim; the correction is carried in print rather than by rewriting the master.

questions.q: "Twenty-seven men bought land." What does the annotation say that line compresses?
options: Nothing; 27 men jointly bought the original tract

It merges the August 15, 1887 incorporation vote, at which 27 registered Black electors voted and elected officers, with the separate land purchases: Clarke's 22 acres from Eaton and a jurisdiction of 112 acres by incorporation
The 27 were the Hungerford trustees
The 27 refers to the town council of 1902
questions.explain: The annotation untangles the compression: 27 electors casting a vote is one documented event, buying land is another, and the line blends them.

questions.q: How are Hurston's books handled in this chapter's source list?
options: Quoted in full as public domain texts

Listed as primary literary sources (among them Mules and Men and Their Eyes Were Watching God) and noted as copyrighted, since Hurston died in 1960, so they are used as summary and brief quotation only
Excluded because fiction cannot be a source
Cited only through the festival's retellings
questions.explain: The copyright and attribution notes state the handling rule plainly: copyrighted primary sources are summarized and briefly quoted, and photographs are linked, not reproduced.

questions.q: What flag does Section 9 raise about the Perplexity master thread's Eatonville segment?
options: It gives the wrong incorporation date

It carries the strong form of the first-town claim, "oldest self-governing Black town in the United States," which conflict 1 narrows; the dossier treats it as evidence of how the claim circulates, not as support for the broad form
It attributes the founding to the wrong Eaton
It omits the Hungerford school entirely
questions.explain: Section 9 agrees with the thread on the date, the 27 voters, Hungerford, and Hurston, and flags the one point where its language outruns the narrowed claim.

timeline.label: Rosewood is settled in Levy County; sources divide between the two years, and the dossier chooses neither
A post office and a Florida Railroad depot are established
The first church (white) is built
The AME church is established; Pleasant Hill AME follows in 1886
By about this year the red cedar is exhausted, the Cedar Key pencil mills close, and most white families leave
The Black community is the majority in Rosewood
The state census counts 355 Black and 345 white residents in the Rosewood voting precinct
The Goins family has wound down its Levy County operation and moved to Gainesville
January 1 to 7: mob violence destroys Rosewood; the official record documents eight deaths
The story returns to the public record through newspaper reporting in the early 1980s, notably Gary Moore's
The state-commissioned historians' report is delivered (December 22)
The Rosewood claims bill (House Bill 591) passes in April: $150,000 to each living survivor
Rosewood is designated a Florida Heritage Landmark and the state marker is placed on State Road 24
Mary Hall Daniels, the last known survivor, dies on May 2 at 98

questions.q: Which statement about Rosewood is accurate?
options: It was incorporated in 1870 and still has a town government
It was a predominantly Black, unincorporated community destroyed in January 1923 and never rebuilt; the site is now a Florida Heritage Landmark
It survives today as a small town near Cedar Key
It was relocated to Gainesville after 1923
questions.explain: The header records Rosewood as destroyed: burned and abandoned in January 1923, never resettled, and designated a Florida Heritage Landmark in 2004.

questions.q: Why did Rosewood's population become predominantly Black by 1900?
options: The state ordered white families to leave Levy County
By about 1890 the red cedar was exhausted and the Cedar Key pencil mills closed, so most white families moved out, selling or leasing their land to Black buyers
A new railroad brought Black settlers in 1900
The town voted to exclude white residents
questions.explain: The chapter ties the shift to the cedar economy's end: the mills closed, white families left, and land passed to the Black families who stayed and bought.

questions.q: When were Rosewood's post office and railroad depot established?
questions.explain: The hamlet had a post office and a Florida Railroad depot from 1870, and the county opened a one-room school in the same era.

questions.q: What role did the Goins family play in Rosewood's economy?
options: They ran the white-owned general store on the railroad line
Their naval stores company distilled turpentine and rosin, they owned or leased several thousand acres, and they became the second largest landowners in Levy County
They owned the Florida Railroad depot
They founded all three of the town's churches
questions.explain: The chapter credits M. Goins and Brothers with the turpentine enterprise, the landholdings, and housing in the section called Goins' Quarters.

questions.q: Why must the 1915 census figure of 355 Black residents be repeated with care?
options: It was a journalist's estimate, not a census
It counts the Rosewood voting precinct, an area larger than the village, so it must not be published as the village's own population
It was taken after the town was destroyed
It includes the population of Sumner
questions.explain: The chapter repeats the caveat each time the figure appears: precinct numbers describe a larger area than the village of Rosewood itself.

questions.q: What does the chapter say is the honest summary of Rosewood's peak?
options: A wealthy boomtown rivaling Greenwood
A rural Black community where families owned land, ran businesses, worshiped in their own churches, and schooled their own children; the ordinariness is the point
A company town owned by the pencil mills
A peak that cannot be described in any respect
questions.explain: The chapter deliberately resists boomtown language: Rosewood's height was self-sufficient, landowning, institutionally complete rural life.

questions.q: Why was Fannie Taylor's January 1, 1923 accusation important in causing Rosewood's destruction?
options: It was proven in court within days
The accusation was never substantiated, but suspicion fixed on an escaped convict and armed posses began searching; the search escalated into a week of killings and the burning of the town
It brought federal troops who burned the town
It persuaded residents to abandon the town voluntarily
questions.explain: The chapter states the sequence plainly: an unsubstantiated accusation, a posse search, the siege at the Carrier house, and by January 7 the remaining Black-owned buildings burned.

questions.q: What did the state's own record later show about the official response?
options: Sheriff Walker controlled the mob and arrests followed
Sheriff Robert Elias Walker did not control the mob, Governor Cary Hardee took no forceful action, a special grand jury indicted no one, and no one was ever prosecuted
The governor sent the militia on January 2
The 1923 grand jury convicted the mob's leaders
questions.explain: The chapter records the failure of protection as part of the event itself, closing with the February 1923 grand jury that found insufficient evidence to indict anyone.

questions.q: What did Florida's 1994 Rosewood claims bill do, and why was it a first?
options: It apologized but appropriated nothing
It appropriated $2.1 million, including $150,000 to each living survivor, and was the first time a U.S. state legislature compensated survivors of racial violence
It rebuilt the town on its original site
It created a state park at Rosewood
questions.explain: House Bill 591, signed by Governor Lawton Chiles in April 1994, paid nine or more identified survivors (the count conflicts across accounts) and funded descendant property claims and scholarships.

questions.q: How did Rosewood's story survive the decades of silence after 1923?
options: In Florida school textbooks of the 1930s
Mainly inside the families, until newspaper reporting in the early 1980s, notably by Gary Moore, returned it to the public record
Through the 1923 grand jury's published findings
The story never went silent
questions.explain: The chapter says the survivors scattered and often never spoke of Rosewood even at home; journalism in the 1980s, then the 1993 state report, restored the record.

questions.q: What physically remains of the 1923 town today?
options: The full historic district, fenced and interpreted
One surviving house, the John Wright house, privately owned, and the state historical marker on State Road 24
The Masonic Hall and two of the churches
A rebuilt village center on the original streets
questions.explain: The chapter is plain about the absence: the Wright house and the 2004 marker are what stand, and the emptiness of the site is itself part of the record.

questions.q: How does the annotation characterize the Rosewood song?
options: A detailed chronicle naming the victims and dates
An elegy, not a chronicle: it names no person, gives no date, and states no death toll, so nothing in it can conflict with the record
A protest song demanding prosecution of the mob
A summary of the 1994 claims bill
questions.explain: The annotation says the song mourns the silence around Rosewood rather than attempting its history, and is therefore treated as an elegy on its own terms.

questions.q: The lyric "Families scattered, erased from the map" matches which documented fact?
options: Survivors rebuilt together elsewhere in Levy County
Survivors left by train and on foot, settled in Gainesville, Tampa, Jacksonville, and elsewhere, and never returned to live in Rosewood
The state removed Rosewood from its maps in 1924
The families moved as one group to Tulsa
questions.explain: Section 5 documents the permanent dispersal the line describes: evacuation by the Bryce brothers' train, shelter at the Wright house, and no return.

questions.q: Which document does the chapter call the controlling official account of January 1923?
options: The Literary Digest's February 1923 coverage
"A Documented History of the Incident Which Occurred at Rosewood, Florida, in January 1923," the 1993 report to the Florida Board of Regents
Wilson Hall's 1994 testimony
The 2004 historical marker text
questions.explain: The chapter identifies the state-commissioned 1993 report as the controlling official account, the document on which the 1994 claims bill rested.

questions.q: How does this dossier handle the disputed death toll?
options: It adopts the highest survivor figure
It carries the documented eight deaths, names the higher survivor claims (up to 27) as claims, and adopts no higher figure as fact
It declines to mention deaths at all
It averages the documented and claimed figures
questions.explain: Conflict 3 records the toll openly: eight documented in the 1993 report, higher figures present in testimony and retelling, none of them adopted.
